comments.author: GyroGhost
comments.textOriginal:
our exact setup converts fine, it uses the 3 MSP slots:

set msp1uart = VCP
set msp2uart = UART1
set msp3uart = UART3
set osduart = UART3

The real problem is a 4th MSP port: master already rejects the 131073 line there, and the OSD gets no port. Dropping the MSP slot always is not safe, because the serial lines come before osddisplayportdevice in a diff, so the conversion cannot know yet whether the OSD is MSP DisplayPort. I will update the PR so that when no MSP slot is free, the line still applies and the OSD takes the port without one.

comments.author: GyroGhost
comments.textOriginal:
our manual setup works because you set OSD Protocol = MSP yourself, so osduart alone opens the port as MSP.

The conversion reads the serial line before osddisplayportdevice, so it cannot know the OSD will be MSP DisplayPort yet. Keeping the MSP slot opens the port as MSP whatever the OSD device ends up being, without changing the user's OSD settings. Only when no slot is free does it select MSP DisplayPort instead, because otherwise the line would be rejected.

comments.author: GyroGhost
comments.textOriginal:
To answer your question on #15764: yes, it looks like the same root cause. Point 2 there states that with landingdisarmthreshold at its default of 0, nothing other than the "quiet velocity" timer disarms an autopilot / GPS Rescue landing.

That timer resets on any transient, so a quad that bounces, skids or flips over on the ground never satisfies it, and the motors keep running. Your blackbox matches that: near-zero ground speed, but an inverted, vibrating quad.

Note that autodisarmdelay won't help here, since it only applies with MOTORSTOP e…

4K-pidloop + dshot300.

4k allows the system more "time" to perform all the tasks (features, filters, etc). 8k-pidloop allows less time to perform all the tasks.

- DShot600 Frame Time: 25–27 µs packet duration. Intended for 8kHz loops (125 µs window).
- Recommendation: DShot300. DShot600 offers no speed advantage at 4kHz because motor updates are thro…

Thanks for narrowing it down — that was the key data point.

What I found

DJI V1 hardware (original Air Unit, Air Unit Lite, Vista, Goggles V1/V2) does not use MSP DisplayPort. That is why O3/O4 are fine and V1 is not — and it matches your photos exactly, where DJI's own overlay still draws but the Betaflight cell-voltage element is gone.

That reply has been growing, and V1 stops accepting it past the 4.5 shape:

AI Generated comment

That's intended, not a new bug: BEEPERUSB suppression only engages with no battery present (bench scenario), matching 2025.12.4 pre-regression behavior exactly. With both USB and battery connected, the beeper sounds by design. Changing that to suppress regardless of battery would reintroduce the original #15423 symptom for battery-powered flight with USB attached (e.g. logging while armed).

Open to suggestions if different behavior is wanted here — may be outside this fix's scope.

comments.textOriginal:
Thanks for the detailed report and video.

The symptom — raw mag data looks correct in Sensors tab but fused heading snaps back — points to an interaction between the IST8310 driver and the IMU's post-rotation attitude reset.

Background

When disarmed, the IMU runs a gain state machine after detecting rotation:
1. During rotation: dcmKpGain drops to 0.25 (mag correction is weak)
2. 250ms quiet period after rotation stops: gain stays at 0.25
3. 500ms reset phase: gain spikes to 25 (100× normal) to quickly converge attitude

If stale mag data is…

t's still broken.

If the GYRO alignment needs to be set to 180° on roll or pitch, then the compass is working in reverse.
If you point the copter north and then move it to the right, the heading increases — but one second later it decreases by the same amount twice.
So if the heading is 0°, and you yaw left to 90°, it will then show 270° after a second. It points west instead of east.

Partial workaround: 
Set the board alignment to 0 / 0 / 0, calibrate the GYRO, then change the alignment to 180° on roll. After that, the compass rotates correc…

I don't know if you are able to make the text shorter, if not, the final solution will be to modify the layout to be able to adjust to larger texts, if possible, but it's not a RTL issue and will happen in more places.

comments.textOriginal: Most probable situation is a power brown-out in your aircraft. In those cases, the model usually hits the ground before the receive can boot back up. If your BEC is not up to the task, then large servo movement under heavy load (due to stress on the control services during high speed) can cause the voltage to drop low enough to trigger a brown-out or power cycle.

comments.author: pkendall64
comments.textOriginal: The quick fix is to have a 1k pulldown resistor on the servo signal wire. This will stop the Servo pulling GPIO12 high during boot which tells the ESP32 that the flash voltage is 1.8V which is too low for the ESP32 PICO-D4 (which is used by these receivers), as they require 3.3V for their internal flash.

comments.author: pkendall64
comments.textOriginal:
This is actually not a bug, it is designed this way.

When a Serial or PMM signal is detected, the auto-detect driver main class creates the appropriate driver and changes the point to that new driver. The underlying drivers do not exit and recreate the auto-detect. This was done mainly because the Serial (CRSF) driver needs to be able to detect the baud rate that is current, ant the user can change baud rate at any time on the handset (EdgeTX).

Yes, ESP8285 is not the right choice for a PWM receiver as it only has 2 timers and no other peripherals that can generate pulses with hardware timing. We have to use a single timer and repurpose it for all the servos in software, which has variable interrupt latency and also the problem of trying to juggle multiple outputs with sub-microsecond accuracy. ExpressLRS receivers based on the ESP32 (all official RXes with more than 5 outputs) use hardware to handle servo PWM and therefore have much more accurate timing.

which then fails with "Not Enough Space" because the 1MB flash needs the
compressed OTA image.

IS8285, and copyhtml.py selects a dedicated web- -tx-8285.h header for

comments.author: pkendall64
comments.textOriginal:
Changing the receiver number on the radio changes the configuration slot on the TX module.
The only information we are given from EdgeTX is a CRSF message to change the receiver number. So we load the configuration from the slot and that will have the default values if the slot has not been used before. If the slot has been used before then the values saved in the slot are used. There is nothing else we can do or we can know at this point.

The problem arises when the RX does not successfully receive the sync packet. This leads to the TX sending 6 bit values, and the RX trying to read them as 7 bit.

comments.textOriginal: The channel value changing only affects Wide switch mode, but the tlm ratio changing does affect everyone. If you're running 100Hz Full 16 channel mode, that's 50Hz (then subtract the set telemetry ratio). The instant you want to transfer MSP, the link drops to 50Hz symmetrical, or 25Hz of channels/control packets. If it is 333Hz Full, then it goes to 166.5Hz in 16ch mode, or 83.25Hz of channels packets when MSP is queued on the TX.

comments.textOriginal:
Speaking of 5 seconds, that's how long this Burst mode typically lasts IIRC. When we need to send a sync packet (which occur on the first time the frequency hopping is on the "sync" channel after every 5 seconds) if there's MSP queued, it will request the other side go to the faster telemetry speed and will stay at that rate until the next sync packet.

So basically 4 MSP calls every 5 seconds will keep the link in "burst" transfer mode constantly.

Just saw this Issue when I was about to file an issue on 900Mhz Mavlink with QGC.

I have a perfectly working setup with 2G4.
RM TX12MK2 internal ELRS + BetaFPV ELRS lite receiver both 2G4 ELRS 3.5.1 and Backpack 1.5.1.

Check your firewall, port 14550 must be open, port 14555 may be a high latency link which does not support mavftp and parameters.

On the other hand the 900Mhz system is completely broken for me.

comments.textOriginal:
Set up an Access Point on your PC and have the ELRS TX connect to it by 
default. This is easily done via Configurator before flashing.

I assume you're on linux.

sudo ufw allow 14550/udp

will open up port 14550. You can limit it to a specific network device.

Delete your manually set connections in QGC, select the option to 
autoconnect on UDP and restart QGC.

Everything should work after that.

comments.author: pkendall64
comments.textOriginal:
Yes, 250Hz used to work on 115200, but a platform update for fix some other issues meant that 250Hz would not work anymore on 115200. So we had to lower the max packet rate for lower baud rates. Some work was done to optimise the pipeline in 3.4 so an internal module can do 250Hz on 115200, but an external module is limited to 200Hz.
If you are interested you can read the PR the did some of the optimisations #2772

comments.author: JyeSmith
comments.textOriginal:
This is probably because the sbus pad requires inverted, while the tlm output from the FC in non inverted.

So you can either have inverted crsf which will give you RC input to the FC, and only the 10 sensors from the Rx.

Or non inverted, and RC will not work but you get all sensors from the FC.

The Rx can not do inverted RC and non inverted tlm input. 

Your other option is to find the non inverted input to the FC for the sbus pad. This is a FC manufacturer question.

comments.author: pkendall64
comments.textOriginal:
I thought I'd do some investigation into this issue, and it appears that TeamRace is really only supported on serial connections for flight controlled devices. It just happens to do some of the work related to TeamRace on the the ER6 because it has a serial port defined by default, whereas the ER5 does not. Hence why the servos don't actually go into failsafe position when using the ER6.
If you can give us a use case as to what you are using the team race feature for with PWM controlled models, then perhaps we can create a feature request issue…

comments.author: pkendall64
comments.textOriginal: I have been able to reproduce this issue on the bench. It appears to be a power issue causing the config part of the flash (which also contains the power-reset counter) to be reset. This is because as part of the startup we increment the power counter and write to config. The problem is that the ESP erases the flash sector before rewriting it. If the power is removed during that phase (due to a spike etc) then the config is gone and you see the behaviour you are getting.

Thanks for the report — confirmed on V14 / V14LCD.
Cause: On STM32F4, VBAT is ADC1-only. Sampling RTC battery in the MAIN multi-channel DMA scan gives a wrong 1.0 V reading.
Fix: Sample RTCBAT alone on ADC1 (EXT), and move MAIN analogs to ADC2 . PR coming shortly.

comments.author: raphaelcoeffic
comments.textOriginal: The main reason is that 2.11 uses a new LUA version so that scripts need to be recompiled. This uses notoriously more memory than just loading the compiled script into memory. Compiling the scripts on simu (which is now actually possible) side steps the compilation process on radio and thus allows to start the script with less memory available.

There is no telemetry TO rx, there is telemetry FROM rx. 

From ELRS faq: TQly | Downlink - link quality (valid packets) | 0 - 100 | An LQ indicator of telemetry packets received by TX. RX → TX

After an esc receives a spool from the fc and rcpulses come back to zero again the esc disarms and forces the user to rearm turtle mode again, but only on the motor pair involved.

title: Sine startup can re-engage mid flight on hard brakes (motor spinning fast), causing desyncs
solutionSummary: I like sine startup. I think it is also a good safety feature, the motors don't spin fast on arming. But I found that on big brakes it can kick in mid flight. For example with the new position hold in Betaflight, or a hard flip stop in acro. Setup: iFlight Blitz E55 4in1 (G071, target IFLIGHTBLITZG071), AM32 2.21, 6S, 2807 1400KV, 7.5" 3-…

comments.author: sevet
comments.textOriginal:
Suggested fix: only re-arm sine startup after a full stop.

Once the motor has started and handed over to BEMF commutation, sine mode should stay off until the motor has really stopped (for example running == 0 after the BEMF timeout). A low throttle on a spinning motor would then stay in normal commutation, and sine startup still protects arming and restarts from standstill.

In code terms: only set steppersine = 1 inside the if (!running) branch, not for every input < 127. I have not tested this change yet.

comments.author: AlkaMotors
comments.textOriginal:
Just to clarify.
Dshot 0 is what betaflight sends on power up. If you want motors to stop send dshot 0. This arms both am32 and blheli32 esc's. 
Dshot 0 is also sent before commands by betaflight. 
All dshot values below 48 and above 0 are dshot commands.
Dshot is a digital signal . We don't need two different values for 0 throttle. 
If leds are all white they have not been programmed most likely or it's the wrong target for your esc.

comments.author: AlkaMotors
comments.textOriginal:
This also matches how regular servo inputs have always worked. To arm any esc send it 0 throttle. To stop any motor from spinning send it 0 throttle too.
Is the issue that blheli32 uses dshot 0 as motor stop and also dshot 48 as motor stop? Am32 does not. There only needs to be one motor stop. We don't need more that one dshot number to represent the same function?
If you put betaflight fc in 3d mode the signal it sends when the motor is to be not spinning is dshot 0. Not dshot 1024 or 48. 
Dshot 0 is always to be no spinning , motor stop.

Support for this chip is already in INAV, it just hasn't reached a build you can flash yet.

comments.author: breadoven
comments.textOriginal: It's not really clear what's happening here. INAV won't disarm because the GPS drops out. Sounds more like a Failsafe which indicates the RC link is being lost. Assuming there is no Failsafe then the controls locking up would indicate a basic Emergency landing, i.e. controls go to fixed positions and the motor cuts out. However, this would only happen if you were using a Nav mode. A log would be most useful. Use Blackbox(MSC) mode from Configurator CLI page to access the log file, it's much faster to download.

comments.author: sensei-hacker
comments.textOriginal:
If you're losing receiver signal and GPS at the same time, you may be flying through a strong RF signal. Look around the area for towers.

In particular, a strategic early warning radar a kilometer away will blow them both out completely. (And you'll piss off the folks running the radar, if you weren't supposed to be flying there). Didn't ask me how I know.

comments.author: sensei-hacker
comments.textOriginal: Closing as resolved by analysis: the blackbox log (posted by the reporter) shows the mid-flight control loss was a receiver failsafe triggering emergency landing — not GPS/compass dropout. GPS loss does not affect controls in manual/angle mode without Nav modes active. Recommended action is a failsafe procedure change (e.g. RTH instead of land) and checking for RF interference. Thanks for the log!

comments.author: daijoubu
comments.textOriginal:
Can you post your diff files please?
In general, MSP Displayport does not tell the video system where to draw the OSD. It tells the video system to draw each character relative to row 0, column 0 but lets the video system define where row 0, column 0 should be drawn relative to the video.
Did you do a full erase when upgrading to 9.1 and then re apply your diff?

comments.author: daijoubu
comments.textOriginal: This is the problem. The reference voltage for the avatar VTx is 12v higher than the reference voltage for the Nexus, assuming the BEC is not isolated and is referenced to battery negative. Because of that, the VTx sees -12 or -9 volts on the Rx pin which is not a valid signal level for a serial UART. From the perspective of the Nexus, the Avatar is putting 12 to 15 volts on it's Rx pin, both of which are well above the threshold to be considered a high, so if it survives, it does not see any change at all on the line.

comments.author: daijoubu
comments.textOriginal: Keep following all the steps in the calibration. Sometimes the first step or two will reset because it set a value for the gain/offset that would not work with the later steps. The orientations shown in the configurator are relative to the arrow on the FC, not the frame of the aircraft. You may have trouble doing it in the aircraft if the arrow on the FC points at an edge, not a corner.

comments.author: sensei-hacker
comments.textOriginal:
> The barometer provides the current altitude reading

Any barometer can only ever tell you something about the difference between two heights/ altitudes.
It measures the air pressure at one point, then measures the air pressure at another point. The difference in pressures allows you to estimate the difference in altitude - if the pressure went down, that's probably because the altitude went up. (Or because the weather is changing).

It is mathematically impossible to know anything about altitude from a single barometer reading.

 Poor positioning of the tube on the model will effect its accuracy.

Virtual airspeed.

- When overheating protection, the LED flashes at 1Hz (the VTXL LED will be off).
- When pitmode, the LED blinks at 2Hz.

titleOriginal: Sequre H743 V2 — Complete 2 MB flash loss after battery power cycle
solutionSummaryOriginal:
I’m investigating a recurring failure on a Sequre H743 V2 flight controller running ArduCopter 4.7.2. 
 The aircraft operates normally, but following an ordinary battery disconnect/reconnect, the controller occasionally fails to boot. 
 Using STM32CubeProgrammer, I captured the entire 2 MB flash memory. Every byte reads FF , including the bootloader and both flash banks. 
 I also have a complete known-good flash image for comparison. Read protection remains at Level 0. 
 The failed controller has not been reflashed because I want to preserve its condition for further diagnostics. 
 Full technical evidence and the exact failure sequence are documented here:

comments.author: xfacta
comments.textOriginal: I would say you can have whatever Yaw PIDs work provided there are not yaw oscillations and during yaw operations the motor outputs are not saturated. Generally saturation is prevented by MOTYAWHEADROOM,200 so you would want to be looking for that headroom to be met quickly (as soon as yaw is commanded) and that may indicate PIDs are too high, or ATCACCYMAX is too high.

titleOriginal: Copter-4.6.1 released!
solutionSummaryOriginal:
Copter-4.6.1 has been released as the official/stable version for multicopters and helicopters. 
 The changes vs 4.6.0 are in the release notes and copied below 
 
 Bug Fixes 
 
 
 Prevent firmware erasure on boards using flash for parameter storage 
 bootloaders rebuilt for H7 boards using flash for parameter storage 
 
 So there is really just one fix which is to do with occasional firmware wipes on boards the store parameters in flash memory . 
 Most users will not see any functional difference between 4.6.1 and 4.6.0. 
 Thanks for those who helped us investigate this problem and we will begin 4.6.2 beta testing early next week!

titleOriginal: Mission Planner 3.0: rewritten cross-platform UI (Windows + Linux, native .NET 10)
solutionSummaryOriginal:
Hi everyone, 
 I’ve been working on Mission Planner 3.0, a rewrite of Mission Planner’s user interface. It runs natively on Windows and Linux, and macOS support is in progress. The first preview build, 3.0.2b, is ready for testing. 
 Why a rewrite? 
 Mission Planner is built on Windows Forms and .NET Framework. That works well on Windows, but on Linux and macOS it needs Mono, which is slow and has rendering glitches. Mission Planner 2.0 keeps Mission Planner’s MAVLink, parameter, mission and vehicle libraries and replaces only the UI layer with .NET 10 + Avalonia. So: 
 
 Native on every platform: no Mono and no Wine. The same app runs on Windows and Linux. 
 Fast: the window opens in about 2–3 seconds, and the HUD, map and telemetry update…

title: Twitching during Takeoff after enabling INS_HNTCH_HMNCS 3 on a Quadcopter
solutionSummary: I recently built a new quadcopter. The initial test flights went smoothly, but after I enabled INSHNTCHHMNCS = 3 , the craft began to twitch violently the moment I armed it and advanced the throttle for takeoff. I immediately brought it down for a landing and disarmed it. The flight controller is a ZeroOne X6Air. I have the log file—could someone help me analyze it to determine the cause? I’ve since changed the parameter back to 1, but I haven’t attempted another test flight yet.

comments.author: MartinRob
comments.textOriginal:
If you have an Ego sensor on the bench you can get it to send messages just by applying 12-15V to VBUS and ground. The balanced output will appear on D+ and D- but the signals swing between 0 and 3V so you don’t really need a balanced receiver to look at them. 
 If you pull the USB CC signal to ground the transmission will stop. This is used to detect and control collisions on the bus but came in handy for disabling the sensors too.

title: Wheel Encoder Input Voltage on Pixhawk 6X
solutionSummary: Hello everyone,In the wiring diagram provided in the ArduPilot Rover documentation, the A and B outputs of the wheel encoder are connected directly to the Pixhawk, and the encoder supply voltage (VCC) is specified as 3.5 V to 20 V.According to the Pololu encoder specifications, the HIGH logic level of the A and B output signals is equal to VCC.My questions are:What is the maximum allowable input voltage for the wheel encoder signals on the Pixhawk 6X GPIO pins?Should the input signal voltage be

comments.author: Yuri_Rage
comments.textOriginal:
Those pins are 3.3 volt TTL/digital IO pins. You may get away with driving them at up to 5V (but don’t if you can help it). 20V will destroy them. 
 I think a 3.5V Vcc should be fine. I’m not sure why you would even try to supply anything above that. 
 I’d try 3.3V first. 3.5 is a very strange spec, and I suspect it might be the result of poor technical translation.

The easiest way is to use two resistors if you know the exact output voltage or two resistors and Z-Diode (3.3V) if the output voltage can shift. 
The resistors are used as voltage divider and the Z-Diode as clamping diode for the FC input pin (between GPIO and GND)

 Use the motor test to test the motors.

 This comes up every week on this forum and is a very common beginner mistake. So don’t worry lots of other users also get this wrong.

A rocket-shaped VTOL is usually a tailsitter: it hovers on its tail and pitches over into forward flight. Both PX4 and ArduPilot can fly that class of airframe. comments.textOriginal: At Indeema we’d keep the flight controller doing flight only and treat the Jetson as a companion that sends setpoints over MAVLink. That way a crash in your vision stack can’t bring the aircraft down. Before flying, try it in SITL with recorded video. (I work at Indeema.)

titleOriginal: ULog crash analysis: how do you identify the first causal failure instead of the final failsafe?
solutionSummaryOriginal:
I’ve been looking at several PX4 incident logs recently, and one pattern keeps coming up: the most visible failsafe or termination event is often not the event that actually initiated the failure. 
 For example, in one recent analysis the vehicle eventually exceeded 80° attitude and entered failsafe. Looking only at the final events could easily make the failsafe or tilt threshold look like the cause. 
 But reconstructing the ULog chronologically showed a different sequence: 
 
 commanded attitude remained small, 
 measured attitude began diverging from the setpoint, 
 actuator outputs subsequently reached extremes, 
 the vehicle continued losing attitude control, 
 failure detection asserted later,

comments.author: dakejahl
comments.textOriginal:
Exactly. High vibration causes aliasing and is the primary cause for this behavior. 
 
 I recommend hard mounting and setting up digital notch filters with ESC RPM feedback. Soft-mounting is tricky because your spring mass damper system will always have a natural resonant frequency susceptible to excitation. Although on larger vehicles you may need to use an isolation system to avoid clipping.

comments.author: LabCD_ai
comments.textOriginal:
That warning comes from loadmon. On NuttX it checks one task per cycle and warns when the task’s unused stack, measured as a high-water mark, drops below 300 bytes. So 244 bytes left means dataman’s deepest call so far came within 244 bytes of the end of its stack. It has not overflowed, but the margin is thin. More reads and writes do not add up; one deep call through the file system sets the mark, which would explain why you see it around mission transfers.

comments.textOriginal:
The diagonal RPM split is usually the mixer doing its job, not a second problem. On a quadrotor, the two motors that spin the same way sit on one diagonal. A non-zero yaw command speeds that diagonal up and slows the other down, which is exactly the RPM pattern you are seeing. 
 If the aircraft is holding heading and yaw rate is near zero in the hover, the controller is just trimming out a constant yaw moment. A little of that is normal. I would only look at motor tilt if that trim is large and persistent, and after the easier mechanical checks…

comments.textOriginal: The 1.4 factor is suspiciously exactly 14/10. The X6 SE-280KV is 24N28P, i.e. 14 pole pairs; if the ESC firmware assumes 10 pole pairs (20 poles), it would report RPM as actual × 14/10 = 1.4×. Start with a complete all-up weight, then check whether the propulsion can hover that weight with enough reserve, and only then estimate flight time.

comments.author: lijiangxing
comments.textOriginal: I work on propulsion hardware at ISWFA, so this question comes up a lot. Start from the all-up weight: add camera, mount and electronics to the bare frame, then look up what your motor/prop combo actually pulls at your target voltage. Total thrust should sit comfortably above that AUW — 2:1 is a reasonable floor for control margin, and below about 1.6 it starts feeling sluggish and slow to react. Frame stiffness and prop clearance matter as much as raw thrust once you add mass. What’s your estimated AUW and frame size right now?

comments.author: JulianOes
comments.textOriginal:
Pixhawk 2.4.8 refers to hardware. The software would be PX4 or ArduPilot. This forum is for PX4. If you’re using MissionPlanner, you would be using ArduPilot (see discuss.ardupilot.org ). 
 A 4in1 ESC usually has 4 connectors to interface to any flight controller. You then usually get the choice between PWM, DShot, or something else as a protocol. PWM and DShot both work with PX4 or ArduPilot.

A pitot tube sitting in the prop wash or close to the fuselage boundary layer, or a bad tube or line, can read low no matter how many times it’s recalibrated. titleOriginal: VTOL Failing to Transition to Fixed Wing
solutionSummaryOriginal:
Hello! I am having an issue with a custom VTOL airframe, it is failing to transition to fixed wing due to not meeting the transition minimum airspeed. I have swapped our airspeed sensor and re-calibrated multiple times. I will attach a ulg of our recent failed flight as well as the current parameter configuration. Any suggestions/advice would be appreciated!
